abstract: Nanopore-based sensing has emerged as a transformative approach for biomarker detection, offering label-free, single-molecule analysis with exceptional sensitivity and specificity. By monitoring ionic current modulations as individual molecules traverse biological or solid-state nanopores, these platforms provide direct insights into molecular size, structure, charge, and interactions. Over the past five years, advances in nanopore fabrication, surface engineering, and signal interpretation have expanded their analytical scope, from nucleic acids and proteins to peptides and small metabolites, while enabling operation in complex biological matrices. This review focuses on recent advancements (from last 5 years) that enhance detection performance and specificity through recognition strategies, engineered pore chemistries, and data analysis. Applications are discussed across key disease areas, including cancer, cardiovascular, neurological, metabolic, and infectious diseases, emphasizing early detection, multiplexed measurements, clinical adaptability and translational diagnostics, highlighting progress toward portable, point-of-care systems. Collectively, these developments underscore the potential of nanopore biosensing to bridge fundamental research and real-world diagnostics, paving the way for rapid, sensitive, and accessible health monitoring tools in precision medicine. Material stability and reproducibility
Long-term stability of solid-state nanopores is a persistent challenge. For instance, silicon nitride nanopores often undergo pore enlargement due to electrolyte-driven etching [
145
]. Surface coatings such as hafnium oxide have been shown to mitigate these effects, but scalable fabrication of stable nanopore arrays is still in its infancy.

Introduction
The global healthcare landscape faces unprecedented challenges from both communicable and non-communicable diseases (NCDs) [
1
], necessitating innovative diagnostic technologies that can deliver rapid, accurate, and accessible detection capabilities. According to the most recent data from the World Health Organization and Global Burden of Disease studies, NCDs currently account for approximately 71% of all deaths globally [
2
], while infectious diseases continue to pose significant threats, particularly in resource-limited settings where they remain leading causes of death. Recent reports from indicated that tuberculosis has resurged as the highest-burden disease worldwide, with approximately 8.2 million people newly diagnosed in 2023, and measles cases increased by 20% from 2022 to 2023, reaching an estimated 10.3 million cases globally [
2
–
4
].
Biomarkers serve as cornerstone indicators in diagnostics and modern medicine, providing invaluable insights into disease states, therapeutic responses, and patient prognosis [
5
]. These objectively measured biological signatures have revolutionized clinical decision-making by enabling early disease detection, monitoring treatment efficacy, and facilitating personalized therapeutic approaches [
6
,
7
]. The significance of biomarker detection extends beyond individual patient care to encompass public health surveillance, disease outbreak monitoring, and population-level health management [
5
]. Early detection through biomarker identification can substantially reduce healthcare costs while improving patient outcomes, as evidenced by studies showing that early intervention can prevent disease progression and reduce the need for complex treatments [
8
].
Traditional diagnostic methodologies, while foundational to modern medicine, present significant limitations that hinder optimal patient care. Conventional approaches such as enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA), polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and culture-based methods often require extensive sample preparation, specialized laboratory infrastructure, trained personnel, and considerable time for result generation [
9
]. These constraints translate into delayed diagnoses, increased healthcare costs, and limited accessibility in resource-constrained environments. Furthermore, traditional methods frequently demand large sample volumes and may lack the sensitivity required to detect low-abundance biomarkers that appear in the early stages of disease [
10
]. To address these challenges, biosensors have emerged as promising alternatives, offering rapid, user-friendly operation and the ability to detect a wide range of analytes including, antibiotics [
11
], pesticides [
12
–
16
], proteins [
17
–
19
], disease biomarkers [
20
] and pathogens [
21
] with high specificity and sensitivity. Biosensing, but through nanopore-based approaches has gained particular attention as they are highly sensitive, label-free, and versatile tool, representing a transformative approach that overcomes many of the inherent limitations of conventional diagnostic methods [
22
,
23
]. The conceptual foundation of nanopore sensing traces back to the Coulter counter principle, originally developed by Wallace Coulter for counting blood cells [
24
,
25
]. This resistive-pulse sensing mechanism has evolved dramatically, transitioning from microscale applications to nanoscale detection capabilities that can identify individual molecules, viruses, and biomarkers with unprecedented precision. Modern nanopore systems operate on the fundamental principle of monitoring ionic current modulations as target analytes translocate through nanoscale pores, generating characteristic electrical signatures that enable molecule identification and quantification [
26
,
27
]. The evolution of nanopore technology represents a major shift in biosensing, offering several compelling advantages over traditional methods. Key benefits include label-free detection, eliminating the need for complex sample preparation and fluorescent tags; real-time monitoring capabilities that provide immediate results; single-molecule sensitivity enabling detection of ultra-low concentrations; and portability that facilitates point-of-care applications [
22
,
28
–
33
]. These characteristics make nanopore sensors particularly attractive for applications requiring rapid, sensitive, and accessible diagnostic solutions.
The urgency for advanced biomarker detection is particularly pronounced in the context of communicable and non-communicable diseases. Infectious diseases (communicable diseases), including emerging infectious agents and antimicrobial-resistant pathogens, require rapid identification to prevent transmission and guide appropriate treatment decisions [
34
,
35
]. The COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the critical need for rapid, accurate diagnostic tools that can be deployed in diverse settings. Similarly, non-communicable diseases such as cardiovascular disease [
36
,
37
], cancer, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease benefit significantly from early biomarker detection, as these conditions often progress asymptomatically in their initial stages [
38
,
39
].
Nanopore sensing applications in disease detection have demonstrated remarkable versatility across multiple domains. In infectious disease diagnostics, nanopore systems have shown capability for pathogen identification, antimicrobial resistance monitoring, and viral load quantification [
40
]. For non-communicable diseases, these platforms have enabled detection of cancer biomarkers, cardiac markers [
41
], and metabolic indicators with sensitivities approaching clinical requirements [
42
,
43
]. The technology’s ability to distinguish between closely related molecules makes it particularly valuable for differential diagnosis and biomarker panel analysis.
This comprehensive review examines the current state and future prospects of nanopore-based sensing for biomarker detection, with emphasis on translational diagnostic applications. We begin by exploring the fundamental principles underlying different nanopore types and their detection mechanisms, followed by an analysis of strategies for enhancing specificity through DNA carriers, aptamer functionalization, and surface chemistry modifications. The review then provides an in-depth examination of recent advances in nanopore-based detection of both communicable and non-communicable disease biomarkers, highlighting successful applications and emerging opportunities. Finally, we address current challenges in the field and discuss future perspectives for advancing nanopore technology toward widespread clinical implementation.
The scope of this review focuses specifically on developments from the past five years, a period marked by significant technological advances and increased clinical validation studies. By synthesizing Fundamentals of nanopore sensing, recent progress in nanopore sensing technology and biomarker detection for diagnostic applications, this review aims to provide researchers, clinicians, and technology developers with insights into the transformative potential of nanopore-based sensing for next-generation biomarker detection and precision diagnostics.
Nanopore types and detection principles
Biological vs. solid-state vs. hybrid nanopores
Nanopores, which are used fabricate sensor can broadly categorized into biological (Fig.
1
a, top), solid-state (Fig.
1
a, bottom), and hybrid nanopores (Fig.
1
b), each offering distinct structural and functional attributes that influence their applications in sensing [
44
,
45
]. The development of these technologies has been a focus of extensive research, especially in recent years [
46
,
47
].
Biological nanopores
Biological nanopores are naturally occurring protein channels, such as α-Hemolysin (α-HL), Outer Membrane Protein G (OmpG), Mycobacterium smegmatis Porin A (MspA), Aerolysin (AeL), Phi29 DNA Packaging Motor (Phi29 Motor) and Cytolysin A (ClyA). These are embedded within lipid [
47
,
48
] except for a Phi29 Motor. In addition to these widely studied biological nanopores, a newly reported anthrax nanopore has expanded the repertoire of biological pores with promising sensing capabilities. This pore was constructed from protective antigen (PA) components of
Bacillus anthracis
and demonstrated stable conductance properties and tunable sensing performance [
49
]. Importantly highlighted the role of the Hofmeister effect in regulating nanopore stoichiometry and assembly, showing that specific ions can influence pore formation and stability. Structures of all these nanopores are presented in Fig.
1
c.
These protein pores possess precisely defined, atomic-scale dimensions, which are crucial for achieving high spatial resolution in single-molecule detection, particularly for DNA sequencing applications [
48
,
50
]. Their inherent structural uniformity facilitates consistent sensing environments, leading to reliable signal generation [
48
]. Beyond naturally occurring protein channels, de novo protein design has yielded membrane-spanning pores with programmable geometry and conductance, enabling tailored biosensing platforms that overcome limits of native scaffolds. Alpha-helical two-ring pores show close agreement between design and structure and support selective ion conduction with strong K
+
preference, while larger 16-helix designs permit passage of small fluorophore conjugates, demonstrating controllable size exclusion for sensing applications [
51
]. Complementarily, de novo β-barrel nanopores with sculpted cross-sections and strand counts produce quiet, stable single-channel currents that scale with pore diameter, opening routes to low-noise detection of analytes beyond DNA [
52
].
Building on these pore-design advances, recent work integrates de novo designed ligand-binding modules to transduce recognition events into robust ionic readouts within such engineered pores. Recent advances in shape-complementary pseudocycle design generate high-affinity binders to diverse small molecules (e.g., cholic acid, thyroxine, methotrexate) and explicitly couple binding to downstream signal transduction for sensing [
53
]. By splitting pseudocycles into independently folding domains and embedding them within designed β-barrel pores, ligand addition reassembles the binder and gates ion flow, yielding low-noise ligand-responsive nanopores exemplified by a CHD-gated TMB12_3 construct with prolonged closed-state dwell times upon analyte binding [
53
]. Together, these computational design frameworks greatly expand the designability of biological nanopores from pore architecture to binding transduction, offering modular routes to biomarker-specific sensing with high specificity and tunable performance.
Biological nanopores are valued for their exceptional molecular recognition capabilities due to their well-defined structures and the potential for chemical modification [
48
]. They enable rapid, label-free, and amplification-free detection of analytes with high sensitivity [
54
]. Despite these advantages, biological nanopores are limited by their relatively low mechanical and chemical stability, making them fragile and less compatible with harsh or diverse experimental environments [
45
,
50
,
55
]. This fragility can restrict their operational durability and broader applicability in certain diagnostic settings [
50
].
Solid-state nanopores
Solid-state nanopores are synthetic channels fabricated in robust membrane materials, including silicon nitride (Si
3
N
4
), graphene, molybdenum disulfide (MoS
2
), and other two-dimensional (2D) materials [
50
,
55
,
56
]. These engineered nanopores offer significant advantages in terms of mechanical strength, thermal as well as chemical stability, and ease of modification, which present them as versatile alternatives to biological nanopores [
55
]. A key feature of solid-state nanopores is their tunable pore size, which can be accurately controlled from sub-nanometers to hundreds of nanometers based on specific experimental requirements, providing greater adaptability than biological counterparts [
55
]. This tunability allows for precise tailoring of sensitivity and selectivity for different target analytes [
50
]. Traditional solid-state membranes, such as silicon nitride, often have thicknesses of several nanometers, which can lead to multiple bases being present simultaneously within the detection zone, thereby limiting single-base resolution in applications like DNA sequencing [
56
]. However, the emergence of 2D materials like graphene and MoS
2
as membrane materials has addressed this limitation, offering thicknesses down to a few atomic layers [
55
,
56
]. MoS
2
has particularly gained traction due to its superior mechanical strength, as well as favorable optical and electronic properties compared to silicon nitride, promising high spatial resolution for DNA and protein sensing [
56
]. Apart from these, the classical quartz glass nanopore and nanopipettes are also part of solid state nanopores. Recent research on solid-state nanopores has also focused on their integration with other technologies, such as optics, plasmonics, and microfluidics, for more complex tasks and chip-scale integration, enhancing convenience and performance [
57
,
58
]. Challenges remain in achieving optimal signal-to-noise ratios and precise control over translocation speed to improve signal quality [
59
].
Hybrid nanopores
Hybrid nanopores represent a strategic fusion of biological and solid-state nanopores (as shown in Fig.
1
b), aiming to leverage the strengths of both systems while mitigating their individual limitations [
44
,
45
]. This approach typically involves inserting biological pores, such as α-HL, into solid-state membranes such as MoS
2
or Si
3
N
4
[
44
]. By combining the high spatial resolution and precise molecular recognition capabilities of biological nanopores with the enhanced mechanical robustness and tunable fabrication properties of solid-state platforms, hybrid systems strive to offer a more versatile and durable sensing solution [
44
,
45
]. This synergy improves the applicability of nanopore sensors for complex biomolecular analyses where both durability and resolution are critical [
13
]. While less explicitly detailed in recent literature compared to individual biological and solid-state types, the concept of hybrid nanopores is recognized for its potential to broaden the utility of nanopore sensing technology [
60
]. The distinct characteristics of each nanopore type are summarized below in Table
1
.

Signal generation and interpretation
Nanopore-based sensing relies on a fundamental principle where the translocation of individual molecules through a nanoscale pore, modulates an ionic current flowing across the pore [
63
,
64
]. This modulation generates characteristic electrical signals that are meticulously monitored over time [
63
–
65
]. The basic experimental setup for nanopore sensing typically involves two compartments (cis and trans, as depicted in Fig.
2
a) of electrolyte solution connected solely by a single pore with a diameter ranging from 1 to 50 nm. When a target molecule diffuses into and passes through the nanopore, it physically occupies some of the space within the pore, excluding a certain volume of conducting ions [
58
,
63
]. This exclusion results in a measurable decrease, or blockade, in the ionic current (Fig.
2
b, c,d), which is directly related to the molecule’s volume and its residence time within the pore [
57
,
63
]. Nanopore techniques are highly sensitive, capable of detecting biomolecules in the nanomolar concentration range within a detection volume as small as 10
−21
liters [
57
].
Types of signals produced
The signals generated by nanopore sensors primarily manifest as transient pulses in conductance via current-time traces (Fig.
2
c, d) [
65
,
66
]. These signals encode abundant information about the translocating analytes, derived from the interactions between the analytes and the nanopore [
46
,
58
]. The key features extracted from these current blockades include:
Current blockade amplitude (blockade level)
This refers to the magnitude of the drop in ionic current, which is indicative of the size, volume, and charge of the translocating molecule [
4
,
57
]. Larger molecules or those with specific shapes tend to cause more significant current blockades [
67
,
68
]. For example, studies have shown that different fibrinopeptide A (FPA) derivatives and conformations can be characterized by unique electrical signals for their blockade level [
69
].
Dwell time
This is the duration for which the ionic current remains blocked, reflecting the time a molecule spends translocating through or interacting with the nanopore [
57
,
59
,
70
]. Dwell time can provide insights into the molecule’s conformational state, its interaction kinetics with the pore, or its folding/unfolding dynamics [
69
]. The phosphorylated form of FPA, for instance, has been observed to adopt two different conformations, each exhibiting distinct dwell times [
69
].
Complex fluctuations or multi-level events
Beyond simple blockades, the ionic current traces can show complex, high-frequency fluctuations or multiple distinct current levels [
71
,
72
]. These intricate patterns can reveal detailed information about a molecule’s conformation, post-translational modifications, or binding interactions within the nanopore [
69
,
71
]. For example, the detection of ovarian cancer marker peptides using gold nanoparticles resulted in complex, high-frequency current fluctuations that provided improved selectivity [
71
]. The precise recognition of multi-level current blockage events (signatures) is crucial for accurate detection of cancer biomarkers [
72
]. Recent studies have also shown that the ionic environment plays a decisive role in regulating such multi-level events. For instance, nanopore measurements performed in asymmetric ionic liquids enabled the discrimination of large and small hepatitis D antigens as well as antigen–ribozyme complexes, highlighting how ion composition can modulate current fluctuations at the single-molecule level [
73
]. Similarly, introducing a cation-coordinated environment with K⁺/Ca²⁺ significantly improved the resolution of carbonic anhydrase detection in MspA nanopores, producing stable and distinguishable current modulations even at very low concentrations in urine samples [
74
]. These findings underscore that tailored ionic environments, through asymmetric ionic liquids or selective cation coordination, represent powerful strategies to regulate multi-level current events and expand the scope of nanopore-based biomarker sensing.
Signal interpretation and data analysis techniques
The raw ionic current signals are inevitably affected by noise, making signal processing an inseparable component of nanopore sensing to identify hidden features [
75
] and analyze them effectively [
46
,
76
]. Recent advances in signal interpretation have significantly enhanced diagnostic accuracy and biomarker detection [
59
,
77
].
Signal processing flow
The signal processing flow for nanopore sensors typically involves several stages, including noise reduction, event segmentation, and feature extraction [
46
]. Noise is ubiquitous and can hinder the detection of minute yet important signals [
76
]. Techniques such as adaptive thresholding, multi-function noise reduction, and segmentation algorithms are employed to isolate single-molecule events with a high signal-to-noise ratio [
59
]. For instance, deep learning approaches have been reported to denoise ionic current signals, enabling the detection of subtle wavy signals that were previously undetectable [
28
]. Increasing the recording bandwidth while maintaining the signal-to-noise ratio is also crucial for resolving fast-translocating molecules [
57
].

Feature extraction and statistical analysis
Once individual events are isolated, meaningful features are extracted from the current blockades, such as central moments and specialized feature sets [
59
]. These features are then analyzed statistically to classify molecules [
59
]. For example, rigorous analysis of data from nanopores has demonstrated the ability to discriminate proteins based on their size, shape, and dipole moment [
78
]. Specific electrical parameters derived from dwell time and blockade level can be used to discriminate peptides from a mixture [
69
]. Chi-squared and autocorrelation analyses have been used to characterize complex current fluctuations, yielding significantly improved selectivity compared to traditional open-pore analysis [
71
].
Machine learning (ML) integration
Machine learning approaches have been increasingly integrated into nanopore data analysis pipelines to improve resolution and identification specificity [
46
,
79
,
80
]. ML-based algorithms systematically evaluate the underlying architectures and properties of signals [
46
]. These methods help to mitigate signal variability introduced by molecular conformation, pore size heterogeneity, and experimental conditions, enabling multiplexed sample analysis under diverse settings [
59
]. Machine learning is being utilized for tasks such as denoising and the classification of various biomolecules [
46
,
76
]. The combination of solid-state nanopores and artificial intelligence holds promise for redefining disease detection and treatment [
80
].
Novel detection mechanisms
Beyond traditional ionic current measurements, innovative detection mechanisms have been developed to overcome challenges such as testing bandwidth limitations and noise, which often lead to the loss of critical translocation signals [
59
]. These include optical detection, tunneling current detection, and nanopore field-effect transistor (FET) detection [
59
]. Nanopore FET sensors, in particular, stand out for their high signal-to-noise ratio and high bandwidth measurement capabilities, addressing limitations typically associated with traditional solid-state nanopore technologies [
59
]. The ability to monitor single molecules provides nanopore sensors with the potential for quantitative sensing based on molecule counting [
66
].
Strategies for enhancing specificity
Enhancing the specificity of nanopore-based sensing is crucial for accurate biomarker detection, particularly for distinguishing between closely related molecules in complex biological samples [
81
,
82
]. Recent advancements have focused on several innovative strategies to improve the selective recognition of target analytes, including the use of DNA carriers, aptamer/antibody functionalization, and modifications to nanopore surface chemistry [
83
,
84
]. These approaches aim to overcome challenges such as low signal-to-noise ratios and non-specific interactions that can hinder precise detection [
85
,
86
]. For example, as shown in Fig.
3
a, functionalizing ATP with tetrahedral DNA nanostructure-supported aptamer (TDN@ATP) produced distinct blockade signals, indicating enhanced event detection [
85
]. Following are the strategies which has been incorporated to enhance the specificity of nanopore-based sensing.
By DNA carriers
DNA carriers are increasingly employed in nanopore sensing to selectively report the presence of target analytes, enabling sensitive assays for molecules that are otherwise difficult to detect, such as small or weakly charged proteins [
86
]. This strategy involves using secondary molecules, specifically DNA nanostructures, to capture target analytes and facilitate their translocation through the nanopore, thereby generating clearer and more distinguishable signals [
83
,
86
].
Enhanced signal-to-noise ratio and control of translocation
DNA carriers can significantly improve the current signal-to-noise ratios, which is vital for detecting small biomolecules that may otherwise produce weak signals [
85
,
87
,
88
]. By coating target proteins with DNA polyhedral carriers, researchers have facilitated protein translocation through solid-state nanopores, making it easier to detect proteins with complex conformations and varying charges [
88
]. A recent study demonstrated that DNA scaffold carriers assisted protein translocation through solid-state nanopores, leading to improved signal-to-noise ratios and enabling real-time sample detection [
87
]. Later a method for producing length-tunable DNA carriers from sticky-ended DNA molecules was introduced, offering flexible control over carrier length and enhancing multiplexing potential by generating separable nanopore signals for distinct targets [
86
]. Additionally, these carriers can capture specific targets at pre-designed sites and escort them through nanopores at controlled speeds, enhancing both capability and resolution for specific target molecule detection [
83
]. Further, the developed single strand template shortening strategy (STSS), transforms short oligonucleotide targets into longer single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) with appropriate lengths to generate significant translocation currents, further extending resolution, signal specificity, and target range [
89
].
Controlling molecular translocation dynamics
Controlling the translocation speed of molecules is crucial for high-fidelity detection. A recent study demonstrated that an asymmetric nanopore can improve “molecular ping-pong” (the recapture and re-reading of the same molecule as shown in Fig.
3
b) by promoting recapture in the trans reservoir [
90
]. Linking target molecules to long DNA carriers further reduced diffusion, leading to over 100 recapture events and enabling accurate resolution of nanostructure motifs along a DNA scaffold through repeated detection [
90
]. This approach provides insights into controlling DNA polymer dynamics within nanopore confinement and offers avenues for developing high-fidelity DNA detection platforms [
90
].
By aptamer/antibody functionalization
Aptamers and antibodies, recognized for their high binding affinity and specificity, are frequently used to functionalize nanopore surfaces, significantly enhancing the selectivity of biomarker detection [
84
,
91
,
92
]. This strategy involves immobilizing these biorecognition elements onto the nanopore, allowing them to selectively capture target molecules and produce distinct electrical signals [
81
,
93
].
Aptamer-based enhancement
Aptamers are single-stranded oligonucleotides that can specifically bind to various targets, including proteins, cells, small molecules, and metal ions [
93
,
94
]. Their ability to undergo target-induced conformational changes makes them highly promising for biosensing [
95
]. A recent study successfully integrated amino acid-specific DNA aptamers into interface nanopores with dynamically tunable pore sizes, enabling the detection of specific peptides by slowing their translocation speeds upon recognition [
96
]. This method could differentiate between peptides containing phenylalanine and control peptides with structurally similar amino acids [
96
]. Recently, an aptamer-assisted nanopore strategy was proposed for direct protein sensing, demonstrating high sensitivity (10 pM) for SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein (NP) detection within one hour, revealing a discriminative two-level current blockade pattern when NP binds to an oligonucleotide-tailed aptamer [
97
]. Furthermore, recent research utilized aptamer-functionalized nanopores to study the kinetics of carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) interactions, showing deep and long blockades for CEA molecules compared to bare gold-modified nanopores, beneficial for cancer biomarker detection [
98
].
Antibody and nanobody functionalization
Antibodies and their fragments, such as nanobodies, provide another effective means of enhancing specificity [
81
,
99
]. Nanobodies are single-domain antibodies with high specificity and stability [
81
]. A recent study described a ClyA nanopore functionalized with different nanobodies via a 5–6 nm DNA linker, enabling specific recognition of large proteins such as SARS-CoV-2 Spike, medium-sized HER2 receptors, and small proteins like murine urokinase-type plasminogen activator (muPA) as shown in Fig.
3
c [
81
]. The functionalized pores could stochastically sense Spike protein and HER2 receptor, showing reduced dynamic movement of unbound nanobodies and increased current when engaged with large or medium-sized proteins outside the pore [
81
]. Importantly, sensing performance was unaffected by blood components, indicating potential for clinical detection. Further, in a different research general strategy was presented for directionally immobilizing nanobodies (as shown in Fig.
3
d) onto track-etched nanopore surfaces using copper-free click reactions, allowing for selective detection of various protein analytes such as green fluorescent protein, mCherry, and α-amylase with quantitative dose-response curves [
99
].
Combined aptamer/antibody approaches
Combining aptamers and antibodies can further enhance detection limits and specificity. A study reported nanopore sensing strategy using a customized DNA molecular probe that integrated both an aptamer and an antibody for enhanced single-molecule detection of mpox virus (MPXV) A29 protein [
100
]. The formation of aptamer-target-antibody sandwich structures enabled efficient identification of targets with a limit of detection (LOD) of approximately 11 fM, distinguishing MPXV A29 from closely related proteins directly in biofluids [
100
]. In another study, the integration of aptamers as signal amplifiers with antigen-binding fragments (F
ab
) as receptors improved the detection limit of silicon nanowire field-effect transistor immunosensors for rabbit IgG down to 1 pg/mL in high-ionic-strength conditions [
91
].
Machine learning integration in aptamer functionalized nanopores sensing
Machine learning algorithms can further improve the discrimination capabilities of aptamer-functionalized nanopores. A recent study demonstrated the use of solid-state nanopore sensing with aptamer functionalization to discriminate between α-thrombin and γ-thrombin [
93
]. By post-processing signals with machine learning and training algorithms using seven features and ensemble methods, an accuracy of 98.8% was achieved [
93
]. Later in further research, “ensemble modified aptamers” (EMAmers) were introduced, exploiting the collective recognition abilities of protein-like side-chain-modified nucleic acid ligands for discriminative identification of molecular or cellular targets (Fig.
3
e), achieving high accuracy in blinded unknown protein, bacterial, and cellular sample identification [
101
].
By nanopore surface chemistry
The surface chemistry of nanopores plays a critical role in their sensing performance, directly influencing selectivity, stability, and the range of detectable analytes [
102
,
103
]. Recent research has focused on modifying nanopore surfaces to improve their functionalization and mitigate issues like current drift and analyte sticking [
102
,
103
].
Controlling surface properties
Surface functionalization of nanopores directly determines the effectiveness of quantitative analysis and single-molecule detection [
102
]. Researchers are exploring various covalent reaction strategies, such as amidation reactions, to modify nanopores with small molecules, peptides, nucleic acids, composite molecules, and proteins [
102
]. These methods provide efficient, versatile, and stable modifications for both biological and solid-state nanopores [
102
]. Recently, a solid-state nanopore fabrication approach was demonstrated that focused on surface chemistry during pore formation by modifying controlled dielectric breakdown (CDB) with a chemical additive, sodium hypochlorite [
103
]. This resulted in dramatically different nanopore surface chemistry, including a significantly weaker acid dissociation constant (K
a
) of surface chargeable head-groups, leading to improved performance such as ohmic behavior in electrolyte, stable open-pore current for over an hour, and higher responsiveness to negatively charged analytes like DNA [
103
].
Peptide coatings and viscosity modulation
Peptides are ideal for surface modifications due to their ability to tailor multiple properties through rational design [
104
]. In recent study, a coated silicon nitride nanopores with a dipeptide layer using l-3,4-dihydroxyphenylalanine (DOPA) as an anchoring element, which tightly binds to many surfaces [
104
]. This one-step functionalization significantly increased the nanopore’s lifetime from hours to months and improved current stability by controlling surface wettability and charge.

Enantiomer discrimination
Modifying nanopore surfaces can also enable the discrimination of molecules with identical mass and charge, such as enantiomers. A recent study utilized an AeL nanopore in conjunction with electrical detection to identify vasopressin enantiomers, l-AVP and d-AVP, based on their unique electrical signatures related to their conformations [
106
]. Principal component analysis was then employed to define relevant electrical parameters for identification, and Monte Carlo prediction was used to assign each event type to a specific enantiomer [
106
]. This demonstrated the potential of nanopore surface interactions to provide highly resolved information for challenging molecular distinctions.
Disease areas & applications
Nanopore applications in noncommunicable diseases
NCDs account for the majority of global morbidity and mortality [
2
], with cancers, cardiovascular conditions, neurodegenerative disorders, and metabolic syndromes representing significant healthcare challenges. Early and accurate detection of disease-specific biomarkers is essential for effective intervention. Detection of these by traditional diagnostic methods often require complex processing, expensive reagents, and extended turnaround times. Nanopore-based sensing offers a powerful alternative, enabling label-free, single-molecule analysis with the potential for rapid, point-of-care applications. This section explores how nanopore technologies are applied across major NCD categories, highlighting advances in biomarker detection and their translational potential.
Cancer and oncology applications
Early and accurate detection of cancer biomarkers is of paramount importance in cancer screening, diagnosis, and monitoring treatment efficacy. Cancer biomarkers are found in tumor tissues and body fluids such as blood and urine, and can be classified into three main categories depending on their application: (1) prognostic, (2) diagnostic, and (3) predictive biomarkers. They encompass a wide range of molecules, including DNA, RNA, proteins, enzymes, and other small molecules, and are further classified according to the type of molecule [
107
]. Traditional methods such as PCR, ELISA, and mass spectrometry can detect these biomarkers, but often require extensive sample processing and lack real-time, single-molecule resolution. Nanopore-based sensing technologies address these limitations by enabling direct analysis of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA), microRNAs (miRNAs), methylated DNA fragments, and cancer-associated proteins with minimal preparation. The approaches covered here range from methylation-sensitive nanopore sequencing for epigenetic profiling, barcoded detection of miRNA signatures, to structural and interaction-based protein assays. This section explains how nanopore platforms are being applied for early diagnosis, molecular subtyping, and monitoring of cancer through direct biomarker detection.
In a direction to detect cancer biomarkers, Guo et al. has designed a modular biosensing platform utilizing a biological nanopore, specifically the α-HL nanopore, to simultaneously and quantitatively detect two key cancer biomarkers, vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and matrix metallopeptidase-9 (MMP-9) as well as environmental pH, all within a single assay. The study introduced a triplex DNA-based nanoprobe that combined a VEGF-specific aptamer loop and a stem-forming oligonucleotide conjugated with a peptide substrate for MMP-9 recognition, allowing both targets to generate distinguishable ionic current signatures during their translocation through α-HL. Binding of VEGF induced the opening of the triplex molecular beacon and release of the signal oligonucleotide, which in turn produced characteristic current events, while the presence of active MMP-9 catalyzed the cleavage of the peptide domain, yielding distinct single-stranded DNA signatures. The system leveraged the modularity of the DNA-peptide hybrid design to provide multiplexed sensing, with the added capability of precise pH measurement based on event frequency patterns. Quantification of VEGF was achieved in the range of 0.1–140 nM with a LOD around 0.1 nM, while MMP-9 was quantified from 0.01 to 90 nM with a LOD as low as 10 pM. Notably, the assay demonstrated minimal interference between analytes, enabling accurate multiplexed detection even in artificial urine matrices that mimic clinical samples. This study addressed the challenge of low-biomarker concentrations and sample scarcity in early cancer diagnostics by enabling the simultaneous, interference-free identification of multiple protein biomarkers and cellular microenvironmental factors. The adaptability of the triplex design highlights its potential for the broader multiplexed detection of protein–protein and protein–enzyme networks in translational diagnostics [
108
].
Further, Li et al. established a label-free, enzyme-free nanopore sensing platform utilizing the biological MspA nanopore for the ultrasensitive detection of circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in breast cancer patients. The assay design incorporated a MUC-1-specific DNA aptamer conjugated to a complementary single-stranded trigger DNA (P1), which was released upon binding to breast cancer cells—thereby initiating a cascade strand displacement amplification (SDA) that produced a three-way junction (3WJ) DNA structure. These 3WJ products generated distinguishable and specific translocation signatures when analyzed by MspA nanopore, allowing accurate differentiation of target CTCs. The sensitivity of this platform was remarkable with a LOD of just 5 cells in the current experimental setup, with the quantification showing a reliable linear relationship between event frequency and cell number from 5 to 1,000 cells, an R² value of 0.9958 demonstrating robust quantitative performance. The specificity was validated by the absence of significant signals with control cell types lacking MUC-1 expression, and clinical testing with patient as well as healthy donor samples confirmed high recovery rate (up to 90% at low cell numbers) with good detection accuracy (1.25–22.5 CTCs/mL in clinical breast cancer blood samples). Notably, the entire process required no more than 5 h, marking a substantial reduction in analysis time compared to conventional methods. This MspA nanopore sensor thus offered highly sensitive, rapid, and cost-effective detection of CTCs, with strong translational potential for early breast cancer diagnosis and monitoring [
109
].
In another approach, Sun et al. had developed a cascaded amplification nanopore sensing strategy (Fig.
4
a) for ultrasensitive detection of the cancer biomarker mucin 1 (MUC-1) and CTCs using an engineered M2MspA protein nanopore. The assay integrated multiple amplification steps via copper sulfide and silver nanoparticles, DNA hydrogel, and DNAzyme, with analyte-triggered signal conversion through a triplex-DNA beacon enabling single-molecule detection. MUC-1 or CTCs were first captured by an aptamer-cross-linked DNA hydrogel, releasing Ag nanoparticles; acid and cation exchange then generated Cu²⁺ to activate DNAzyme-mediated cleavage of the triplex DNA substrate, producing distinct nanopore translocation events. This approach achieved a quantifiable range of 0.0005–0.5 pg/mL for MUC1 with an LOD of 0.1 fg/mL, and 5–2000 cells/mL for MCF-7 CTCs with an LOD of 2 cells/mL, all within 6 h. The method showed high selectivity, minimal whole-blood interference, and strong agreement with clinical diagnostic results from 19 patient samples. Despite multiple processing steps, it provides a flexible, cost-effective, and highly sensitive model for detecting diverse protein and cell biomarkers in translational cancer diagnostics [
110
].
Subsequently, Cai et al. established an amplification-free, single-molecule, multiplexed nanopore biosensing platform using solid-state quartz nanopipette nanopores for direct detection of circulating microRNA cancer biomarkers from human serum. The method employed size-encoded DNA carrier probes with molecular beacons that hybridize to target miRNAs, generating a fluorescence signal while producing a distinct ionic current signature during nanopore translocation. This electro-optical dual readout enabled sequence-specific detection, including single-nucleotide discrimination, and multiplexing via DNA barcoding. The platform sensitively detected prostate cancer-associated miR-141-3p and miR-375-3p in as little as 0.1 µL of unprocessed serum, with LODs of 5 fM and 8 fM respectively, under optimized conditions. Clinical validation showed high sensitivity and specificity, effectively distinguishing active disease from remission cohorts and outperforming RT-qPCR in both detection limit and sample volume requirements. The adaptable design supports rapid customization for other cancer-related miRNAs and potentially other nucleic acid or protein biomarkers, offering a promising minimally invasive tool for multiplexed cancer diagnostics and monitoring [
111
].
Later, Cao et al. introduced a solid-state nanopore biosensing platform using a quartz glass nanopore functionalized with a CEA-specific DNA aptamer (Fig.
4
b) for label-free, single-molecule detection and kinetic analysis of CEA. The nanopore’s inner surface was gold-coated and modified with thiolated aptamers via gold–thiol chemistry, enabling selective CEA binding. Each CEA–aptamer interaction generated prolonged, deep ionic blockade events distinct from transient spikes seen with bare or non-targeted pores. Event frequency correlated linearly with CEA concentrations from 0.01 to 1 nM (2–200 ng/mL), allowing extraction of kinetic parameters, including a dissociation constant (K
d
) of 1.28 × 10⁻⁷ M. The platform showed excellent specificity against unrelated proteins (IgG, AFP, BSA, HRP) and maintained performance in complex matrices. In human serum assays, results closely matched ELISA, with the lowest reliably detected and quantified CEA concentration at 0.01 nM. This functionalized solid-state nanopore method offers rapid, sensitive protein biomarker detection and real-time kinetic characterization at the single-molecule level, advancing translational cancer diagnostics [
98
].
Then, Tian et al. developed a sensitive solid-state nanopore biosensing platform for CEA detection using a silicon nitride (SiN
x
) nanopore, aptamer recognition, and DNA nanotechnology for signal amplification. CEA-specific aptamers were immobilized on streptavidin-coated magnetic Fe₃O₄ nanoparticles and hybridized with tetrahedral DNA nanostructures (TDNs). CEA binding triggered TDN release, whose nanopore translocation generated distinctive ionic current blockades, with event frequency correlating to CEA concentration. The assay achieved a 0.06 nM LOD and a linear range of 0.1–10 nM, showing high specificity against PSA, BSA, and thrombin. Validation with human serum yielded recoveries of 97.0–102.2%, confirming robustness in complex matrices. The label-free method leverages the stability and modifiability of solid-state nanopores and DNA nanostructures, offering a rapid, reproducible, and ultrasensitive approach for CEA quantification and early cancer diagnostics [
112
].
Further, Stierlen et al. established a sensor using a wild-type AeL biological nanopore to discriminate single-molecule peptide biomarker derivatives and post-translational modifications, focusing on FPA besides its phosphorylated version FPA-P and cleaved variants linked to coagulation disorders and cancer. The sensor resolved distinct blockade current and dwell time signatures for each form, revealing two conformational populations of FPA-P with unique electrical parameters. This dual-parameter approach enabled accurate identification of FPA, FPA-P, and derivatives in complex mixtures, detecting conformational changes induced by phosphorylation beyond the reach of conventional methods. While LOD and LOQ (Limit of quantification) were not specified, single-molecule detection was achieved at micromolar concentrations, outperforming antibody-based and mass spectrometry assays in speed, specificity, and discrimination of modified forms. The authors suggested further enhancement via machine learning and engineered nanopores to improve sensitivity, paving the way for multiplexed, low-cost peptide biomarker diagnostics [
69
].
Later, Doan et al. fabricated an optical nanopore blockade sensor for ultralow-level detection of VEGF using a high-density solid-state nanopore array with wide-field fluorescence microscopy (Fig.
4
c). In this approach, polystyrene nanoparticles functionalized with anti-VEGF antibodies (Ab-PSNPs) were captured by nanopores modified with anti-VEGF aptamers, forming immunosandwich complexes. Then quantification was achieved by counting nanopores that remained blocked after a reversed electric field, enabling single-molecule resolution and overcoming throughput/noise issues of earlier electrical blockade sensors. The assay detected VEGF at sub-picomolar levels in < 15 min, with a LOD of 78.75 fM and a quantitative range of 78.75 fM–7.89 pM. Here, antifouling silane-PEG-COOH and aptamer modifications ensured high selectivity, maintaining performance in protein-rich backgrounds such as human serum albumin.

Cardiovascular disorders
Cardiovascular diseases remain a leading cause of death worldwide [
114
], where rapid detection of acute and chronic disease biomarkers is critical for timely treatment. Cardiovascular diseases encompass a broad spectrum of acute and chronic conditions in which timely and accurate biomarker detection is critical for diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment monitoring. Conventional protein- and nucleic acid-based assays, while clinically established, often require multiple processing steps and lack the capability to resolve fine structural, conformational, or chemical modifications at the single-molecule level. Nanopore-based sensing offers a unique alternative, enabling direct electrical interrogation of cardiac biomarkers ranging from proteins and peptides to genomic variants. Approaches demonstrated in this domain include proteomic fingerprinting of enzymatically digested biomarkers, peptide–protein interaction profiling for natriuretic peptides, conformational and enantiomeric analysis of vasoactive peptides, label-free detection of inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein, and ultra-rapid sequencing for the genetic diagnosis of inherited cardiomyopathies. This section explains the diversity of nanopore strategies for cardiovascular diagnostics, spanning protein, peptide, and genetic biomarkers.
Initially, Afshar Bakshloo et al. devised the fingerprinting strategy using the biological AeL nanopore to identify water-soluble proteins via the unique patterns of peptide fragments generated by enzymatic digestion. For cardiovascular diagnostics, they demonstrated that myoglobin, a key acute myocardial infarction marker, could be reliably distinguished from proteins of similar molecular weight through reproducible ionic current blockade patterns from its trypsin-digested fragments. The workflow involved protein denaturation, proteolytic cleavage, and nanopore analysis, with fragment populations characterized by normalized residual current (I
b
/I
o
) and blockade duration, yielding label-free qualitative fingerprints without complex preparation. Parallel analyses of lysozyme and cytochrome c further confirmed the platform’s ability to resolve proteins by distinct fragment signatures. This work highlights the AeL nanopore’s potential for rapid, user-friendly detection of clinically important protein biomarkers like myoglobin, supporting broader applications in nanopore proteomics [
115
].
Then, Zhang et al. established an antibody-free, label-free biosensing platform using a biological α-HL nanopore (Fig.
5
a) for single-molecule discrimination and quantification of multiple natriuretic peptides such as ANP (Atrial Natriuretic Peptide), BNP (B-type Natriuretic Peptide), and CNP (C-type Natriuretic Peptide) which are key cardiac biomarkers for heart failure diagnosis. By exploiting peptide–protein interactions within the α-HL nanopore, the system distinguished homologous peptides and cyclic, linear, or chemically damaged variants via measurable current blockade ratios (I
b
/I
o
) and residence times (τ
off
). Molecular simulations confirmed that structural and charge differences governed interaction strength, following the order ANP >CNP >BNP. For clinical translation, BNP detection in complex blood matrices was demonstrated, achieving an LOD of ~ 770 fM using an asymmetric electrolyte assay, which was around 1,597× more sensitive than symmetric assays, well below diagnostic thresholds. The practical range spanned 0.77 pM–1 µM, with the lowest reliably quantified BNP matching the LOD. This approach showcases peptide–protein nanopore sensing as an ultrasensitive, multiplexed tool for cardiac biomarker detection and for monitoring subtle structural modifications relevant to cardiovascular disease [
116
].
Further, Wu et al. introduced a solid-state nanopore biosensing strategy (as shown in Fig.
5
b) for single-molecule detection and conformational analysis of human C-reactive protein (CRP), a key inflammatory biomarker closely linked to cardiovascular diseases, cancer progression, and other inflammatory disorders. Using size-optimized silicon nitride nanopores (14 nm) fabricated via controlled dielectric breakdown, the platform achieved a LOD of 0.3 ng/µL. Voltage polarity experiments revealed that CRP translocation is predominantly driven by electro-osmotic flow under physiological pH, with higher negative bias accelerating translocation but also inducing partial dissociation of native pentameric CRP into pro-inflammatory isoforms and monomers above − 300 mV. pH variation influenced translocation speed via changes in surface charge on both CRP and the pore, but did not significantly alter CRP conformation. The assay also differentiated CRP–aptamer complexes from CRP alone, with aptamer binding altering translocation orientation and current blockage profiles in a concentration-dependent manner. In spiked human serum, the system could reliably detect CRP at 30 nM under physiological conditions. This label-free, single-molecule approach offers high sensitivity, structural insight, and applicability in complex biofluids, making it a promising tool for early diagnosis, prognosis, and monitoring of cardiovascular and other inflammation-related [
117
].
Later, Gorzynski et al. demonstrated the transformative potential of nanopore sequencing technology for the ultra-rapid, genome-wide genetic diagnosis of dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) in a critical care setting. In an adolescent presenting with acute cardiogenic shock of uncertain etiology, the authors deployed a whole-genome sequencing workflow using Oxford Nanopore Technologies’ long-read platform, achieving sample-to-diagnosis turnaround in under 12 h. This included efficient DNA extraction, rapid library preparation, high-throughput nanopore sequencing, and real-time computational analysis, culminating in the identification and clinical confirmation of a likely pathogenic, de novo TNNT2 variant (a gene well established in the genetic basis of DCM) prior to the patient’s transplant listing decision. The study highlights the clinical value of integrating nanopore sequencing for actionable genetic insight in critical and time-sensitive cardiovascular presentations where classical diagnostic modalities (biopsy, imaging, and delayed panel-based sequencing) may be insufficient or untimely. It is important to note that, unlike protein nanopore biosensing approaches which directly interrogate circulating biomarkers such as peptides and cardiac proteins, this work exemplifies the application of nanopore technology as a rapid, flexible sequencing platform for comprehensive genomic analysis. The ability to generate, call and curate clinically actionable variants within a matter of hours underscores the unique advantages of nanopore sequencing for precision medicine in inherited and acute cardiomyopathies, complementing rather than replacing direct biomarker biosensing in the overall landscape of cardiovascular diagnostics [
118
].
Subsequently, Ratinho et al. introduced a wild-type AeL biological nanopore for single-molecule detection and discrimination of peptide enantiomers (Fig.
5
c), focusing on L-vasopressin (L-AVP) and its D-enantiomer (D-AVP), both critical in cardiovascular regulation. For the first time, a native AeL pore sensitively distinguished L- and D-AVP—individually and in mixtures—by their distinct conformational signatures, including saddle and open states in disulfide-bridged peptides, resolved through unique current blockade and dwell time profiles under native and reducing conditions. Discrimination was enhanced via principal component analysis and Monte Carlo classification, enabling confident assignment of signals to specific enantiomers and states. Operating at low micromolar peptide concentrations with single-molecule resolution, the method bypassed mass spectrometry and chromatography limitations by simultaneously providing sequence, conformation, and chirality information in a rapid, label-free assay. This capability to resolve subtle structural and chiral differences highlights nanopore sensing’s potential for early disease diagnostics, drug development, and monitoring racemization or post-translational modifications [
106
].
Then, Zhang et al. developed a droplet nanopore platform for point-of-care detection of angiotensin II, a critical cardiovascular biomarker associated with hypertension and heart failure. Using a microfluidic droplet interface bilayer (DIB) system coupled with solid-state nanopores, the assay operated with only 0.4 µL of sample, achieving a detection limit of 42 pg in a droplet volume of 0.4 µL. The system employed a multichannel array allowing high-throughput, parallel analysis, and formed lipid bilayers within just 1 min of droplet contact, enabling rapid testing suitable for clinical environments. The nanopores demonstrated stable operation for over 5 h, maintaining sensitivity and reliability, while direct analysis from unprocessed droplets eliminated complex sample preparation processes. The assay’s ability to detect angiotensin II at physiologically relevant concentrations highlights its potential as a portable, low-volume, real-time biomarker platform for cardiovascular point-of-care diagnostics, paving the way for improved early detection and monitoring in outpatient and resource-limited settings [
77
].

Neurological disorders
Neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) are driven by molecular events including protein misfolding, aggregation, pathogenic isoform formation, and genetic repeat expansions. Many of these biomarkers are present at low concentrations and in structurally diverse forms, making them challenging to detect with traditional bulk assays. Nanopore-based sensing addresses these limitations by enabling direct, label-free, single-molecule analysis with the capacity to distinguish subtle differences in size, conformation, and sequence in real time.
Applications discussed here include tracking β-amyloid aggregation, multiplexed detection of Alzheimer’s-related protein biomarkers, rapid identification of α-synuclein amyloid seeds in Parkinson’s disease, detection of C9orf72 repeat expansions in ALS, single-cell dopamine monitoring, and nanoscale characterization of tau and tubulin aggregates.
This section explains how nanopore platforms are advancing the detection and structural characterization of neurological disease biomarkers for both mechanistic studies and early diagnostic development.
Initially, Lenhart et al. developed a biological nanopore biosensor using α-HL (Fig.
6
a) for single-molecule monitoring of β-amyloid (Aβ40) aggregation dynamics, a hallmark of Alzheimer’s disease. The system distinguished monomers, oligomers, and larger aggregates via distinct current blockade and dwell time signatures where monomers yielded long, full blockades, while oligomers/aggregates produced brief partial “bumping” events. Tracking of Aβ40 incubated at 4 °C and 37 °C over 20 days, revealed faster, more complete aggregation at physiological temperature. Then quantitative nanopore data correlated with dynamic light scattering (DLS) which enabled real-time mapping of evolving amyloid species. While LOD/LOQ were not specified, the method achieved single-molecule sensitivity, offering higher temporal resolution than bulk assays such as ELISA or mass spectrometry. The authors noted that adaptation to clinical matrices may require immunoprecipitation to address selectivity and fouling issues. This work demonstrates nanopore sensing as a powerful tool for studying protein aggregation, drug screening, and potentially early diagnosis of neurodegenerative diseases [
119
].
Further, Liu et al. demonstrated a label-free, ultrasensitive α-HL nanopore biosensor (Fig.
6
b) for simultaneous detection and discrimination of multiple Alzheimer’s disease biomarkers such as Aβ42, Aβ40, APP669-711 and Tau fragments in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and serum. In the experiment, distinct ΔI
b
/I
o
signatures (Aβ42: 70.4 ± 0.1%, Aβ40: 82.0 ± 0.1%, APP669-711: 91.4 ± 0.1%, Tau: 61.1 ± 0.5%) were obtained, which enabled sequence-level resolution of closely related peptides. The platform achieved real-time multiplexed detection directly in samples from AD mouse models, with results matching ELISA and plaque imaging. Sensitivity reached an LOD of 195 pM for Aβ42 in CSF, improving under ionic liquid-assisted conditions in serum to 2.1 pM (Aβ42), 1.5 pM (APP669-711), and 627 fM (Aβ40). Small-volume CSF analysis captured age-dependent biomarker changes and differentiated 5xFAD AD mice from controls. Offering rapid preparation, high specificity, and single-molecule resolution without labels, this α-HL nanopore system addresses the limitations of conventional assays and shows strong potential for early Alzheimer’s diagnostics [
120
].
Then, Meyer et al. introduced a nanopore-based assay, termed as real-time fast amyloid seeding and translocation (RT-FAST), using solid-state quartz nanopipettes (Fig.
6
c) for rapid, single-molecule detection of α-synuclein (αS) amyloid assemblies relevant to Parkinson’s disease. Here, the confined nanopipette reservoir accelerated amyloid seed amplification (assisted by anti-fouling coatings) while resistive pulse sensing at the nanopore tip enabled high-resolution detection of resulting aggregates. RT-FAST detected αS seeds, including wild-type and pathogenic A53T variants, within 90 min at sub-nanomolar monomer concentrations, far faster than conventional RT-QuIC assays. Quantitative analysis of blockade amplitude, dwell time, and capture rate allowed kinetic profiling and seed quantification down to low picomolar levels. The system distinguished aggregate heterogeneity and mutant seed cross-seeding effects, offering insights into early oligomeric species during the lag phase of aggregation. This label-free, ultrasensitive approach highlights nanopipette-based nanopores as powerful tools for both fundamental Parkinson’s research and potential point-of-care diagnostics [
121
].
Later, Li et al. developed a sensitive nanopore biosensing method combining catalytic hairpin assembly (CHA) amplification with the MspA nanopore for quantitative detection of C9orf72 hexanucleotide repeat expansions (C9-HRE), a key genetic marker for ALS and frontotemporal dementia (FTD). The approach leverages target-triggered CHA to generate double-stranded DNA products that produce distinct ionic current blockades during translocation through MspA, enabling detection of less than 30 repeats which were critical to differentiate healthy individuals from patients. The system exhibited high specificity by discriminating C9-HRE from other repeat expansions and demonstrated robust performance in complex biological matrices including cell and blood samples. The strategy’s label-free, user-friendly nature, together with strong anti-interference capacity, supports its potential as a rapid and accurate clinical diagnostic tool for ALS and related neurodegenerative diseases. Moreover, the platform’s modular design suggests applicability to other disease-related repeat expansions through tailored probe sequences [
122
].

Then, Acharjee et al. built a solid-state silicon nitride nanopore biosensing approach, integrated with atomic force microscopy (AFM), for the detection and characterization of tau and tubulin protein aggregations which are central biomarkers in neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and Pick’s disease. In this method, silicon nitride nanopores (8–30 nm in diameter) were fabricated on silicon membranes and incorporated into a microfluidic system with silver chloride electrodes to measure ionic current changes. When a bias voltage was applied, tau and tubulin proteins in buffered solution translocated through the nanopore, partially obstructing ionic flow and producing measurable current blockades. The amplitude of these current drops was directly related to the size and aggregation state of the protein complexes, enabling discrimination between monomeric and aggregated forms (such as dimers, trimers, and multimers) using variously sized nanopores. Experimental parameters such as bias voltage (60–210 mV) and pH (7.4–12) were optimized to investigate the aggregation behavior and enhance detection sensitivity. The nanopore findings were corroborated by AFM imaging of protein samples, confirming aggregation size distributions and validating the nanopore analysis. This dual-platform strategy demonstrated that solid-state nanopores, when combined with AFM, provide a robust, label-free and sensitive means of monitoring protein aggregation states relevant to neurodegeneration. The study lays the groundwork for further development of rapid, quantitative diagnostic assays for protein aggregation-related neurological disorders [

Metabolic disorders
Metabolic disorders such as diabetes and chronic kidney disease involve complex biochemical dysregulation that can be captured through diverse classes of biomarkers, including disease-specific proteins, enzymatic substrates, metabolic cofactors, autoantibodies, and small-molecule metabolites. Rapid and sensitive detection of these analytes is critical for early diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment monitoring. Various nanopore-based sensing platforms have been developed to address these. Recent advances span the detection of matrix metalloproteinase-2 for diabetic kidney disease (DKD), single-molecule quantification of NAD
+
/NADH ratios for redox state assessment, discrimination of glutamic acid decarboxylase and its autoantibodies in type 1 diabetes, direct serum measurement of glucose and lactic acid stereoisomers, and high-specificity quantification of retinol-binding protein 4 (RBP4) for chronic kidney disease diagnostics. This section explains how nanopore technologies are applied to a wide range of protein, peptide, and metabolite biomarkers relevant to metabolic disorders, with an emphasis on diabetes and renal disease.
Guan et al. established a machine-learning-assisted nanopore biosensing platform using a biological α-HL protein nanopore (as shown in Fig.
7
a) to achieve direct, label-free detection of matrix metalloproteinase-2 (MMP-2)—an emerging indicator for diabetic kidney disease —at the single-molecule level. Their strategy employed engineered peptide substrates with MMP2-specific cleavage sites; after enzymatic digestion, the resulting peptide fragments were analyzed by their distinctive ionic current signatures during nanopore translocation. Assisted by machine learning algorithms for event classification, the system achieved 100% accuracy in distinguishing between substrate and product events, enabling robust quantification across a clinically relevant concentration range (50–400 ng/mL) with a LOD of 17.5 ng/mL. The method maintained high recovery rates in simulated urine, highlighting its potential for DKD diagnosis and monitoring. Notably, the authors also demonstrated inhibitory profiling and high specificity against non-target proteins, supporting the platform’s reliability and translational promise as a next-generation, user-friendly diagnostic tool for diabetes-related renal disease [
125
].
In a study by Liu et al. a single-molecule biosensing platform developed by leveraging a biomimetic molecular clamp integrated into an engineered biological α-HL (α-HL(M113R)7) nanopore for simultaneous, label-free quantification of NAD
+

This approach required no labeling or amplification, allowing real-time monitoring of enzymatic transformations and redox state changes in physiological samples, underscoring its utility as a robust diagnostic tool across metabolic, degenerative, and oncological disease context [

Then, Tao et al. built a label-free, high-throughput platform using quartz glass solid-state nanopores for the single-molecule detection and discrimination of glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD65), glutamate decarboxylase antibodies (GADAb), and their antigen-antibody complexes, key biomarkers of type 1 diabetes. By analyzing ionic current blockade signatures such as translocation amplitude, duration, and frequency, under varying voltages (− 200 mV to − 600 mV), the study distinguished these biomolecules based on their size, charge, and interaction states. The authors observed transient multi-molecule congestion within nanopores at higher voltages, revealing voltage-dependent molecular behavior. Distinction between monoclonal and polyclonal antibodies was achieved via different translocation time and blockade current profiles, demonstrating the sensor’s ability to resolve complex antibody populations. Notably, this immobilization-free method allowed detection of premixed GAD65-GADAb immune complexes, identifying multiple binding states including monovalent and bivalent forms. This facile, reproducible glass nanopore platform offers a cost-effective and sensitive strategy for early screening of autoimmune markers in type 1 diabetes, with potential extension to other immunological diagnostics [
127
].
Later, Jia et al. developed a rapid, label-free biosensing method using a phenylboronic acid (PBA)-modified MspA biological nanopore for single-molecule identification of L-lactic acid, D-lactic acid, and D-glucose directly from human serum (Fig.

After ultrafiltration to remove proteins, serum filtrate was added to the MspA-PBA nanopore, where cis-diols on each analyte reversibly bound to the PBA adapter, producing distinct ionic current signatures. A custom machine learning algorithm enabled accurate discrimination between metabolites, even in complex matrices. The platform detected D-glucose across physiological (~ 5.5 mM), diagnostic (≥ 11 mM), and severe hyperglycemia (≥ 22 mM) levels, and readily measured physiological L-lactic acid (0.5–2.2 mM). Here, LOD was defined as the lowest concentration yielding ≥ 5 diagnostic events within a 10-min recording. This direct, amplification-free sensing covered all medically relevant concentrations for diabetes and lactic acidosis assessment, offering a rapid, low-cost, and high-throughput point-of-care tool [

Further, Chen et al. developed a solid-state nanopore sensing strategy for quantitative detection of retinol-binding protein 4 (RBP4-a biomarker of chronic kidney disease (CKD)) in urine by combining a double-antibody sandwich immunoassay with silicon nitride nanopores. Optimization of buffer composition, voltage, antibody concentration, and pore size (28 nm) improved signal-to-noise ratio and specificity. The method provided a linear detection range of 55 fM–5.5 pM, with the lowest reliably detected concentration at 55 fM. In 11 clinical urine samples, it achieved 100% accuracy in differentiating CKD patients from healthy donors within 40 min. The dual-antibody approach yielded robust and distinct translocation signals, whereas single-antibody assays suffered from signal overlap and poor specificity. Minimal interference from abundant urinary proteins (SAA1, NGAL, S100β) confirmed high selectivity, and results matched fluorescence immunoassay benchmarks. This work demonstrates the potential of optimized nanopore immunosensing for rapid, label-free, and sensitive protein biomarker detection in complex biofluids, offering a generalizable framework for clinical proteomics [
